tiles.title: Prioritizing Findings and Framing Recommendations
tiles.summary: Learn to lead a stakeholder report with the finding most relevant to the decision, frame a recommendation that is distinct from the finding itself, and open the narrative with a short context section that level-sets the reader.

steps.title: Lead with what the decision-maker needs, not what surprised you most
steps.lede: A delivery-times analysis can surface many findings. Choosing which one opens the report is a judgment call — and the right criterion is the stakeholder's decision, not analytical novelty.

blocks.text: A full look at QuickShip delivery times might surface several findings: Lagos slowed down, Kano's times are the most variable, one courier is unusually fast. Not all of them belong at the top of the report to the Head of Operations.

The engagement and scoping stage should establish how the analysis will inform decisions. That decision — whether to add Lagos couriers — points to which finding matters most: the Lagos slowdown, not the courier with the fastest times. Crafting a communication's big idea requires knowing what is not essential and boiling the overall message down to a single sentence that captures its core.

Writing about data should only include information relevant to the audience. The operations manager's decision about Lagos staffing does not require the full breakdown of every city's variability. Relevance to the decision — not analytical novelty — is the right criterion.

blocks.text: Use the inverted pyramid: most important information first, everything else from most to least important. For the QuickShip delivery report, the Lagos slowdown opens the report; other findings follow only if relevant to the decision.

steps.title: A finding tells you what happened; a recommendation says what to do
steps.lede: Restating a finding more emphatically is not a recommendation. A recommendation names the action and what the reader is being asked to approve.

blocks.text: "Lagos delivery times rose to 30 minutes" is a finding — it describes what the data shows. "We recommend adding one more courier to the Lagos route" is a recommendation: it states what should happen next. The two are easy to confuse, but a stakeholder needs both.

The value of analytical efforts is only truly realized when the insights discovered are acted upon. An audience cannot be assumed to find the intended takeaway as obvious as the presenter thinks it is. Simply restating the Lagos finding more emphatically may not tell the manager what to do — the recommendation needs to say so explicitly.

A well-formed recommendation makes clear to the audience what they need to know and what they are being asked to do. "We recommend adding one Lagos courier; please approve the added headcount" states the action and names the explicit ask, so the Head of Operations knows exactly what decision is in front of them.

steps.title: Start with why: set the context before the findings
steps.lede: Before the Head of Operations reads any finding about Lagos delivery times, they need to know why they are reading this report at all.

blocks.text: Before the Head of Operations reads any finding about Lagos delivery times, they need to know why they are reading this report at all. Dropping straight into numbers without context leaves the reader to guess the purpose of the analysis.

In a story's structure, the beginning establishes the context: what is happening, or what the situation is, when the story begins. A summary should have an obvious beginning, middle, and end; the beginning level-sets the audience before diving into the analysis.

A report should not start with lengthy background or technical definitions. Instead, include a short paragraph explaining what the publication is about, with more detailed information placed in a separate section. For the delivery report: "This report looks at delivery times across our three cities last quarter" — not a page of methodology before the findings.

Explaining why the statistics have been collected includes relevant, factual information about the policy and operational context. Noting that this review was prompted by rising customer complaints about Lagos deliveries gives the reader a reason the analysis exists at all.

remediation_steps.lede: A finding describes what the data shows. A recommendation states what action to take and what the reader is being asked to do.

A recommendation is not a louder restatement of the finding — it is a distinct statement of what should happen next.

tiles.title: Sample Size, Effect Size, and Statistical Significance

steps.title: Why Sample Size Changes How Much You Can Trust a Result
steps.lede: Two checkout-button tests both show a 10% lift — but one ran with 50 users per group and the other with 5,000. Should you trust them equally?

blocks.text: A bigger sample tends to provide a more precise point estimate than a smaller sample. The more orders or users you observe, the more accurately you can estimate the effect of the explanatory variable — here, which checkout button a user saw — on the response, whether they completed an order. In a single study, precision comes from collecting a sufficiently large sample.

So the 5,000-user version of the QuickShip checkout test tends to produce a more precise estimate of the button's effect than the 50-user version — even though both happened to show the same 10% lift. The larger test observed far more completed orders, so its estimate of the button's effect is more accurate.

left.title: Estimated lift — small sample
left.alt_text: Number line showing five hypothetical lift estimates from small-sample runs scattered widely from −2% to 25%, illustrating high variability around the true 10% lift.

right.title: Estimated lift — large sample
right.alt_text: Number line showing five hypothetical lift estimates from large-sample runs clustered tightly between 9% and 11%, illustrating low variability around the true 10% lift.

blocks.takeaway: Same 10% lift, very different precision. The large-sample estimates cluster tightly; the small-sample estimates scatter widely. A bigger sample gives you a more trustworthy point estimate.

steps.title: Hypotheses, p-Values, and Statistical Significance
steps.lede: The checkout test showed a 10% lift for the redesigned button. Before recommending it company-wide, you need language for how sure that result actually is.

blocks.text: The null hypothesis (H0) often represents a skeptical position — a perspective of 'no difference'. The alternative hypothesis (HA) represents an alternative claim under consideration. For the QuickShip checkout test, H0 is that the redesigned button makes no real difference to completion rate; HA is that it does.

The p-value is the probability of observing data at least as favorable to HA as the current data set, if H0 were true. It quantifies the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis. Statistical significance measures how unusual a result would be if there were actually no difference between the variation and the baseline and the discrepancy were due to chance alone. The diagram below previews how repeated sampling produces a spread of confidence intervals — a concept covered fully in the next step.

blocks.title: 25 confidence intervals built from different samples (around p = 0.88)
blocks.alt_text: Strip of 25 horizontal 95% confidence intervals built from different samples around p = 0.88. Twenty-four intervals contain the true proportion line; one interval (CI 25) visibly misses it, illustrating that a small fraction of correctly-built intervals will fail to capture the parameter.

steps.title: p-Values and Sample Size in Action
steps.lede: See how sample size drives p-values and why a large sample can make a tiny difference look statistically significant.

steps.title: What a Confidence Interval Actually Means
steps.lede: A confidence interval is not a probability statement about a single interval — here is what it does mean, and two common errors to avoid.

blocks.text: A confidence interval is a range of plausible values likely to contain the population parameter — the true value you are trying to estimate. If many samples were taken and a 95% interval built from each one, about 95% of those intervals would contain the parameter.

Describing a confidence interval as capturing the population parameter with a certain probability is a common error; while it may be useful to think of it that way, the confidence level only quantifies how plausible it is that the parameter is in the given interval. So it is not quite right to say ‘there is a 95% chance the true completion-rate difference is in this interval’ — the 95% describes how the method behaves across many samples, not the probability attached to this one interval.

Not every confidence interval captures the true value, even when the method is followed correctly. In an illustrative set of twenty-five 95% confidence intervals built from different samples around p = 0.88, only one failed to contain the population proportion. A small fraction of correctly-built intervals will miss it.

steps.title: From Confidence Interval to Business Decision
steps.lede: Getting a p-value or confidence interval is not the end of the job — someone still has to decide what to do about the checkout button.

blocks.text: H0 often represents a skeptical perspective or a claim to be tested; HA represents an alternative claim under consideration. The value being compared to the parameter in this setup is called the null value. For the two textbook examples, the null value is p0 = 0.333.

In one example, the null value (p0 = 0.333) fell within the confidence interval computed from the sample — that value was not implausible, so the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject H0. In a second example, p0 = 0.333 was not in the 95% confidence interval, so H0 was rejected: the data provided statistically significant evidence that the proportion differed from 0.333, and because the entire interval was below 0.333, it was concluded to be lower.

blocks.title: Null value inside vs. outside the 95% CI
blocks.alt_text: Two number-line scenarios side by side. Scenario A: 95% CI spans 0.22–0.50, with the null value 0.333 falling inside the shaded band — fail to reject. Scenario B: 95% CI spans 0.09–0.31, with the null value 0.333 falling outside and above the band — reject, conclude proportion is lower than 0.333.

steps.title: Failing to Reject Is Not the Same as Accepting the Null
steps.lede: The first example failed to reject H0 — but that does not mean H0 is true.

blocks.text: Failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to accepting it as true. It only means there was not strong enough evidence for the alternative. In the first textbook example, perhaps there was an actual difference, but it could not be detected with the relatively small sample of 50.

Analyzing a test's results means stating whether the variation had a positive, negative, or neutral effect versus the baseline (control). For the QuickShip checkout test, that means saying plainly whether the redesigned button did better, worse, or about the same as the original — not just reporting a p-value and stopping.

When the sample size becomes large, even a very small, practically unimportant difference can be detected and called statistically significant. An online experiment might find that placing additional ads on a movie review website statistically significantly increases viewership of a TV show by 0.001% — but that increase might not have any practical value. A business conclusion has to weigh the size of the lift, not just whether it was detected.

steps.title: What You Learned
steps.lede: Three ideas that connect sample size, significance, and business conclusions.

blocks.text: A bigger sample gives a more precise estimate. Statistical significance tells you how unusual a result would be under the null — not that the lift is large enough to matter. When the sample size becomes large, even a tiny, practically unimportant difference can be called statistically significant. And failing to reject H0 is not the same as accepting it as true.

remediation_steps.title: Small vs. Large Sample: A Direct Comparison
remediation_steps.lede: Both QuickShip checkout tests showed a 10% lift — but the estimates from the small test scattered widely, while the large test's estimates clustered tightly. That difference in spread is what precision means.

blocks.text: A bigger sample tends to provide a more precise point estimate. With 50 users per group, the estimated lift could easily land anywhere from near zero to well above 20% just by chance. With 5,000 users per group, the same estimate stays close to the true value because far more completed orders are observed. Precision comes from sample size, not from the size of the lift itself.

remediation_steps.title: H0 vs. HA: The Skeptic and the Claim
remediation_steps.lede: H0 is the skeptic — it says nothing changed. HA is the claim you are trying to find evidence for.

blocks.text: For the QuickShip checkout test, H0 says the redesigned button makes no real difference to completion rate. HA says it does. The p-value measures how surprising the observed data would be if H0 were true — a small p-value means the data would be very unusual under H0, giving evidence for HA. A large p-value means the data are not surprising under H0, so there is not enough evidence to reject it.

remediation_steps.title: Null Value Inside vs. Outside the CI
remediation_steps.lede: The decision rule is simple: if the null value sits inside the confidence interval, you cannot reject H0. If it sits outside, you reject.

blocks.text: In the first textbook example, p0 = 0.333 fell inside the 95% CI — the null value was plausible, so the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject H0. In the second example, p0 = 0.333 was not in the CI, and the entire interval was below 0.333, so H0 was rejected and the conclusion was that the proportion is lower. Failing to reject in the first example does not mean H0 is true — it may simply mean the sample of 50 was too small to detect a real difference.

tiles.title: Defining the Question and Planning the Workflow

steps.title: From Vague Complaint to Scoped Business Question
steps.lede: The operations team at QuickShip says deliveries feel slow lately. That is not yet something you can analyze.

blocks.text: Before any analytical work begins, the question to be addressed, its context, and its boundaries should be identified. Turning a vague complaint into a workable target is called scoping. Scoping ensures an appropriate, common understanding of the problem is defined, and that expectations are aligned with what the analysis can produce.

steps.title: Why Every Later Step Depends on the Scoped Question
steps.lede: Every later capstone step — what data to retrieve, how to clean it, what to compute — serves this one sentence.

blocks.text: For QuickShip, scoping the vague complaint means settling its context and boundaries: which orders (a specific quarter's deliveries), which measure (delivery time against a target), and which unit of comparison (delivery zone). The result is a specific business question: 'Which delivery zones are missing the delivery-time target, and by how much, over the last quarter?' Scope it loosely, and the rest of the project has nothing precise to aim at.

steps.title: Matching Each Data Source to Its Retrieval Tool
steps.lede: With the question scoped, the next decision is how to get the data. QuickShip's order records live in a SQL database; the driver roster is kept in an Excel workbook.

blocks.text: Data that lives in a SQL database can be retrieved with a SQL query; pandas' SQL query wrappers (pandas.io.sql) facilitate this retrieval. So the orders table, sitting in the company's database, is a SQL-query job.

read_excel() reads an Excel file directly into a DataFrame. So the driver roster workbook, which never touches a database, is a read_excel() job instead. The capstone ends up using both: a SQL query pulls the last quarter's orders (zone, driver_id, delivery_time_min) from the orders table, and read_excel() pulls the driver roster (driver_id, name, zone, shift) from the spreadsheet.

steps.title: The Six-Stage Analytical Workflow
steps.lede: With the question scoped and both retrieval tools chosen, sketch the whole project's shape before touching either one.

blocks.text: An analytical project is commonly structured through phases that begin with scoping the question and end with delivering and communicating the results. A phase such as scoping may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations — for example, if cleaning the orders data reveals that 'last quarter' is ambiguous in the source system, that sends you back to re-scope rather than pressing on.

Within that structure, the source data is retrieved (via a SQL query or a spreadsheet import), and data quality should be assessed at every stage, with quality improvements such as cleaning focused as early as possible. So right after the orders query and the roster import, the capstone checks for problems like missing delivery times — rather than waiting until the final analysis to discover them.

steps.title: Modeling Multi-Table Data and Communicating Results
steps.lede: Two stages of the workflow deserve special attention: modeling (when data spans more than one table) and delivery.

blocks.text: Where the project's data spans more than one table, the modeling stage connects related tables; relationships are what connect related information between tables. The capstone's orders and drivers are two such tables, so a modeling stage links them — using driver_id as the join key — before any deeper analysis relies on both together.

In the delivery and communication stage, insights are communicated to the commissioner and approver — the people who need them. Activities may include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and presentations. The capstone's version of this is reporting the zone-delay findings back to the operations team that raised the original complaint.

remediation_steps.lede: A scoped question has three parts: what you will measure, which records you will use, and what the analysis will not answer.

blocks.text: Before any analytical work begins, the question to be addressed, its context, and its boundaries should be identified. For QuickShip, the context is last quarter's orders and the boundary is delivery time by zone — not every possible cause of delay. Scoping ensures you and the operations team share the same understanding of what the analysis will and will not answer.

remediation_steps.lede: The retrieval method is not a preference — it follows where the data actually lives.

blocks.text: Data that lives in a SQL database is retrieved with a SQL query via pandas.io.sql. Data stored in an Excel workbook is read with read_excel(). For QuickShip: the orders table lives in the company's database (SQL query), and the driver roster is an Excel workbook (read_excel()). remediation_steps.title: The Workflow Is Not a Straight Line
remediation_steps.lede: Any stage can send you back to an earlier one — that is a feature, not a failure.

blocks.text: An analytical project commonly runs Scope → Retrieve → Clean/Model → Analyze → Visualize → Communicate. But a phase such as scoping may need to be revisited if a later phase encounters changes or limitations. If cleaning the orders data reveals that 'last quarter' is ambiguous in the source system, that sends you back to re-scope the question rather than pressing on with a flawed definition.

steps.title: Running the Whole Plan Yourself
steps.lede: With the plan, retrieval, cleaning, modeling, statistics, and visualization steps all defined, what is left is carrying the whole thing out yourself — end to end — without being walked through each step again.

blocks.text: During the design phase, the commission is converted into an analytical plan, with some iteration expected as the solution is developed. For the capstone, the workflow outline from earlier becomes that analytical plan, and it is normal to adjust it once the SQL, spreadsheet, and pandas work actually starts.

During the analysis phase, the planned analysis is carried out while progress and relevance are monitored, and appropriate records of the analysis conducted, changes, decisions, and assumptions made are maintained. As the capstone's query, cleaning, modeling, statistics, and figures get built, a decision log captures what changed and why.

steps.title: Turning Findings into a Story for the Operations Team
steps.lede: The finished analysis now needs to be turned into something the operations team can act on: a narrated stakeholder summary of what was found.

blocks.text: Designing a communication with a specific person in mind — even if that is not always the reality — can help avoid treating a 'mixed audience' as one undifferentiated group. Knowing what motivates that audience lets you frame what you need them to know or do in those terms. So instead of writing for 'the operations team', write for the Head of Operations specifically.

steps.title: Beginning, Middle, End — and What Counts as Sufficient
steps.lede: A summary can follow a story structure with an obvious beginning, middle, and end.

blocks.text: The beginning level-sets the audience with the big picture and background context. The middle presents what the analysis found. The ending gives the key takeaway — such as a recommended next step. For the QuickShip capstone, the beginning sets the delivery-time target, the middle reports the Lagos slowdown, and the ending recommends adding one courier to the Lagos route.

During delivery, insights are communicated to the people who need them, sufficiently for them to determine whether the work meets their requirements. This communication can include summary packs, reports, or presentations. For the capstone, the finished summary pack should let the Head of Operations judge whether the analysis answers the original question.
A narrated summary aimed at one specific person, moving through beginning, middle, and end, is what turns the capstone's findings into something its audience can actually use.

steps.title: Write the Narrated Stakeholder Summary
steps.lede: Using the QuickShip zone delivery summary, write a narrated stakeholder summary for the Head of Operations. Structure it with a clear beginning (context), middle (findings), and end (recommendation). Submit your summary pack.

steps.title: Packaging the Work So Others Can Evaluate It
steps.lede: The very last capstone step: package the finished work so someone who never watched it get built can understand and evaluate it.

blocks.text: Transparency about the analytical decisions, process, limitations, and changes made at each stage should be clearly shown through documentation of the analysis, assumptions, and data, together with records of the decisions and quality-assurance checks made. For the capstone, that means documenting the decisions made at each stage — from scoping through visualization.

Delivery and communication activities can include producing summary packs and reports, launching dashboards or websites, and giving presentations. The capstone's deliverable is the finished report or summary pack, together with the visualization set already built, presented to the operations team that raised the original complaint.

steps.title: What You Learned
steps.lede: Three ideas that complete the capstone.

blocks.text: Independent execution is running the whole plan yourself, adjusting it as needed, and keeping a decision log along the way. A narrated summary aimed at one specific person — moving through beginning, middle, and end — turns findings into something the audience can act on. Documenting the decisions made and presenting the finished report and visuals together is what makes the capstone a deliverable someone else can evaluate.

remediation_steps.title: Design Phase vs. Analysis Phase
remediation_steps.lede: Independent execution has two distinct phases — and both produce something.

blocks.text: During the design phase, the commission is converted into an analytical plan, with some iteration expected. During the analysis phase, the planned analysis is carried out while progress and relevance are monitored, and records of the analysis conducted, changes, decisions, and assumptions made are maintained. The design phase produces the plan; the analysis phase produces the outputs and the decision log.

remediation_steps.title: Beginning, Middle, End — Applied
remediation_steps.lede: A story structure makes the summary usable, not just readable.

blocks.text: The beginning level-sets the audience with the big picture and background context. The middle presents what the analysis found. The ending gives the key takeaway, such as a recommended next step. For the QuickShip capstone: beginning — the 25-minute delivery target; middle — Lagos-North and Lagos-South are both missing it; end — add one courier to the Lagos route.

remediation_steps.title: Documentation Makes the Work Evaluable
remediation_steps.lede: A deliverable is not just finished work — it is finished work that someone else can understand and evaluate.

blocks.text: Transparency about the analytical decisions, process, limitations, and changes made at each stage should be clearly shown through documentation of the analysis, assumptions, and data, together with records of the decisions and quality-assurance checks made. Delivery activities can include summary packs, reports, dashboards, and presentations. Together, the documentation and the delivery layer make the capstone a deliverable someone else can evaluate — not just finished work only you understand.
